title: The gospels written down
hookLine: as eyewitnesses aged, their memories were written as the four gospels
last: PRAY FOR THE PEACE OF JERUSALEM.

cards: Who in your family still remembers the oldest stories? The grandmother who knows how your great-grandparents met. The uncle who was there when the house burned.
Sooner or later somebody says: we should write this down. The early church had that moment too. The people who had walked with Jesus wouldn't be there forever.
A letter in Peter's name says it plainly: "I will endeavour that ye may be able after my decease to have these things always in remembrance."
The stories were still told aloud, at tables and in prayers, but the voices were thinning.

teach.b: Luke opens his Gospel like a careful historian: "Forasmuch as many have taken in hand to set forth in order a declaration of those things which are most surely believed among us, Even as they delivered them unto us, which from the beginning were eyewitnesses, and ministers of the word."
Notice what he admits. He isn't the first to try; others have written already. And the stories came from eyewitnesses who delivered them, handed them on, the way tradition works.
Luke writes "in order," so his friend Theophilus might "know the certainty of those things, wherein thou hast been instructed."

Mark has no introduction at all: "The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God." Straight in. An early tradition, preserved by the church historian Eusebius, says Mark wrote down what Peter remembered.

teach.h: THESE ARE WRITTEN, THAT YE MIGHT BELIEVE.
teach.b: John ends with a confession that there's far more: "And many other signs truly did Jesus in the presence of his disciples, which are not written in this book: But these are written, that ye might believe."
And at the very end, almost with a smile: if everything were written down, "even the world itself could not contain the books that should be written."
So the church ended up with four Gospels, under the names tradition gives them: Matthew, Mark, Luke and John. They tell the same Jesus from four angles, and they don't always line up in detail.
The churches kept all four side by side instead of blending them into one, each in its own voice, written down before they forget.

how: Churches read from the Gospels in their services, often standing for the reading, and in several churches the reading plan moves through Matthew, Mark and Luke over a cycle of years, with John read at special seasons.

games.q: you're an early church leader. the eyewitnesses are dying. people tell the stories at every meal, a little differently. what do you do?
o: let the stories stay spoken; writing will spoil them.
write them down, from those who were there.
choose one version and forbid the rest.
games.why: Luke writes "in order," from what eyewitnesses delivered, and the church keeps four Gospels side by side.

practice: Bring to mind someone older who told you a story more than once, a parent, a grandparent, a neighbor, a teacher, and let one story come back: where they were, who was there, what they said at the end.
If you have something to write with, put it down in a few plain lines, the way they told it, without polishing. If you pray, give thanks for the person who told it.

wordCard.voice: Luke. The evangelist who wrote his gospel in order, so Theophilus might know the certainty of what he'd been taught, as the church set its eyewitness memories on paper.

orig.note: Greek: gospel, good news; the word in Mark 1:1.
